lead: After the correlators the receiver holds a point r in signal space, near one of the M signal points but pushed off it by noise. The optimum detector chooses the signal that most probably produced r. In white Gaussian noise with equally likely signals this is simply the nearest signal point, so the decision regions are bounded by perpendicular bisectors. The error probability then depends only on the distances between points and on N₀, through the Gaussian tail function Q(x). These formulas tell a link designer how much energy per bit buys how few bit errors.
prereq: You need: signal space (coordinates and distances) and the correlation receiver.

sections.h3: The received vector and the maximum-likelihood rule

blocks.text: A bank of N correlators, one per basis function, turns r(t) into a vector r = s<sub>m</sub> + w when signal m was sent. In additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) of two-sided density N₀/2, the noise components w<sub>1</sub> … w<sub>N</sub> are independent Gaussian variables with mean 0 and variance N₀/2 each.

The maximum-likelihood (ML) rule chooses the m for which r is most likely. The likelihood of r given sm is proportional to exp(−‖r − sm‖²/N₀), which is largest when ‖r − sm‖ is smallest. So, for equally likely signals:
m̂ = the m with the smallest ‖r − sm‖
Here this is the minimum-distance rule. It is the ML rule in AWGN for any energies; with equal priors ML is also the minimum-error (MAP) rule.

Expanding the distance, ‖r − sm‖² = ‖r‖² − 2⟨r, sm⟩ + Em. The term ‖r‖² is the same for every m, so the receiver can equally compute the correlation metric ⟨r, sm⟩ − Em/2 and choose the largest. Only when all energies Em are equal may the −Em/2 term be dropped, leaving the largest correlation. The worked example shows a case where dropping it gives the wrong answer.

sections.h3: Decision regions and the error of two points

blocks.text: The decision region of sm is the set of all r that are decided as m. Under the minimum-distance rule the boundary between two points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them: on it the two distances are equal. Figure 5.6.1 draws the regions for the three-point set from the Gram-Schmidt example.
Here Q(x) is the probability that a zero-mean, unit-variance Gaussian exceeds x. Q(0) = 0.5, Q(1) = 0.159, Q(2) = 0.0228, Q(3) = 1.35 × 10⁻³, Q(4) = 3.17 × 10⁻⁵, and Q(x) = ½ erfc(x/√2).
For two points a distance d apart, an error happens when the noise component along the line joining them exceeds d/2. That component has variance N₀/2, so
Here d is in V·√s and N₀ in V²·s (W/Hz across 1 Ω), so the argument has no unit.

Polar (antipodal) signalling has points ±√Eb, so d = 2√Eb and Pe = Q(√(2Eb/N₀)). On-off signalling with points 0 and √E has d = √E but an average energy per bit Eb = E/2, so Pe = Q(√(Eb/N₀)): the same error rate needs 3 dB more Eb/N₀. Binary orthogonal signals sit in between at d = √(2Eb), giving the same Q(√(Eb/N₀)) as on-off.

sections.h3: More than two points: the union bound

blocks.text: With M points, signal m is decided wrongly if r lands in any other region. The exact probability needs an integral over the region, but a simple upper bound adds the pairwise errors:
Here dmk is the distance from point m to point k. This is the union bound; it counts twice the noise that crosses two boundaries at once.

At high SNR the nearest neighbours dominate, so Pe ≈ N̄min Q(dmin/√(2N₀)), with dmin the smallest distance in the set and N̄min the average number of neighbours at that distance. Points on a line (M-ary PAM) are worked out in full in correlative coding and M-ary PAM.

examples.question: Polar binary signalling is used at E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 10 dB. (a) Find the bit error probability. (b) Find the E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ that gives P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁵. (c) What would on-off signalling give at 10 dB?
steps: (b) Solve Q(x) = 10⁻⁵: x = 4.265. Then 2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = x² = 18.19, so E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 9.09, that is 10 log₁₀ 9.09 = 9.59 dB.
(c) On-off: P<sub>e</sub> = Q(√10) = Q(3.162) = 7.83 × 10⁻⁴, about 200 times worse at the same E<sub>b</sub>/N₀.

examples.question: Use the three points of the Gram-Schmidt example, s<sub>1</sub> = (1, 0), s<sub>2</sub> = (1, 1), s<sub>3</sub> = (1, −1) V·√ms, equally likely, with N₀ = 0.05 V²·ms. (a) Decide r = (1.4, 0.3) by the minimum-distance rule and by the correlation metric, and show what goes wrong if E<sub>m</sub>/2 is dropped. (b) Find the average symbol error probability.
steps: Correlations ⟨r, s<sub>m</sub>⟩: 1.4, 1.4 + 0.3 = 1.7, 1.4 − 0.3 = 1.1. Energies 1, 2, 2. Metrics ⟨r, s<sub>m</sub>⟩ − E<sub>m</sub>/2: 0.9, 0.7, 0.1. Largest is s<sub>1</sub>, agreeing with the distances.
Dropping E<sub>m</sub>/2 would pick the largest correlation, 1.7, that is s<sub>2</sub>: wrong, because the energies are not equal.
(b) The boundaries are the horizontal lines φ<sub>2</sub> = +0.5 and φ<sub>2</sub> = −0.5, each 0.5 from its neighbours. The noise along φ<sub>2</sub> has σ = √(N₀/2) = √0.025 = 0.158.
One boundary crossing: Q(0.5/0.158) = Q(3.162) = 7.83 × 10⁻⁴. s<sub>2</sub> and s<sub>3</sub> have one boundary each; s<sub>1</sub> has two, so its error is 2 × 7.83 × 10⁻⁴.
examples.answer: (a) r is decided as s<sub>1</sub> (distance 0.500, metric 0.9); the bare correlation would wrongly pick s<sub>2</sub>. (b) P<sub>e</sub> = 1.04 × 10⁻³.

traps: Losing the 2 in the polar formula. Polar binary gives Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)); Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)) belongs to on-off and orthogonal signalling and is 3 dB worse.
Putting E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ in dB straight into Q. Convert first: 7 dB is a ratio of 10<sup>0.7</sup> = 5.01, not 7.
Saying the nearest-point rule needs equal energies. Minimum distance is ML in AWGN for any energies; it is the bare largest-correlation rule that needs equal energies.
Using Q(d/√N₀). The noise variance along a line is N₀/2 and the boundary is d/2 away, which gives Q(d/√(2N₀)).
Reading the union bound as exact. It is an upper bound that is tight only at high SNR.

quiz.q: State Q(0) and explain the value.
quiz.a: Q(0) = 0.5: half the area of a zero-mean Gaussian lies above 0.

quiz.q: Why is the ML rule the minimum-distance rule in AWGN?
quiz.a: The likelihood of r given s<sub>m</sub> is proportional to exp(−‖r − s<sub>m</sub>‖²/N₀). The exponential falls as the distance grows, so the most likely signal is the nearest one.

quiz.q: Describe the decision boundary between two signal points in a 2-D signal space.
quiz.a: It is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining the two points; on it the two distances are equal. On each side the nearer point wins.

quiz.q: Polar signalling is used with E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 8 (linear). Find P<sub>e</sub> using Q(4) = 3.17 × 10⁻⁵.
Two points are 2 × 10⁻³ V·√s apart and N₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁷ V²·s. Find P<sub>e</sub>.
A student uses Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)) for polar signalling when designing for P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁵. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Q(x) = 10⁻⁵ needs x = 4.265. The student sets E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = x² = 18.2 (12.6 dB) instead of x²/2 = 9.09 (9.59 dB), asking for 3 dB more power than polar signalling needs.

quiz.q: Why is polar signalling 3 dB better than on-off signalling for the same average energy per bit?
quiz.a: Polar points ±√E<sub>b</sub> are 2√E<sub>b</sub> apart. On-off points 0 and √(2E<sub>b</sub>) have the same average energy E<sub>b</sub> but are only √(2E<sub>b</sub>) apart, a factor √2 less. Matching the distance needs twice the energy, which is 3 dB.

beyond: Real receivers rarely make hard decisions now: they pass soft values (log-likelihood ratios) to a channel decoder, which gains about 2 dB over hard decisions. Coded modulation, MIMO detection and sphere decoding all reuse the nearest-point geometry of this chapter in more dimensions. Search for soft-decision decoding, log-likelihood ratio and sphere decoder.

figure.caption: Decision regions of the worked example: the boundaries are the perpendicular bisectors φ<sub>2</sub> = ±0.5. The received point r = (1.4, 0.3) is 0.500 from s<sub>1</sub>, 0.806 from s<sub>2</sub> and 1.360 from s<sub>3</sub>, so the receiver decides s<sub>1</sub>, though s<sub>2</sub> has the larger correlation.

spec.aria: Signal plane with points s1 at (1, 0), s2 at (1, 1) and s3 at (1, minus 1). Dashed horizontal boundaries at plus and minus 0.5 split the plane into three bands. A received point at (1.4, 0.3) has distances 0.500, 0.806 and 1.360 to s1, s2 and s3 and lies in the s1 band.
